newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Plavsic battles fellow Bosnian Serb nationalists.
newsitem.headline: Plavsic battles fellow Bosnian Serb nationalists.

text.p: Bosnian Serb leaders who fought a war for the shared dream of an "ethnically pure" state are feuding in peacetime over whether some were distracted along the way by lucrative smuggling rackets.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, as nationalist as any in the ruling party, has nevertheless accused her associates of betraying the soldiers and civilians who fought against Bosnian independence and the multi-ethnic state it promised.
She has taken on the most powerful men in Serb territory -- including wartime leader Radovan Karadzic -- and blasted them publicly for running what she called "shameful" smuggling deals.
"Do they think that the rest of the population will be their slaves?" she said in a speech last week.
Plavsic's campaign against corruption has focused attention on a subject that every Bosnian whispered about but never dared to utter in public.
The conflict has fuelled speculation that major powers are preparing to arrest Karadzic, who has refused to face charges before the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague.

Instead of keeping a low profile as he promised, Karadzic has drawn attention to himself by trying to crush Plavsic. "He may have moved the day of his extradition much closer," said one Western official.
Karadzic loyalists have had difficulty responding to Plavsic's detailed charges and instead have tried to portray her as a pawn of Western governments plotting to undermine the Serbs.

But her credentials as a hardline nationalist make it difficult for Karadzic loyalists to smear her. The mood has been euphoric among her supporters in the industrial centre of Banja Luka, which has long resented being ruled by a small circle based in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo.

Even Moslem and Croat opposition politicians who harbour no affection towards Plavsic have welcomed her effort to expose corruption. An opposition party in the Moslem-Croat Federation has called on authorities to divulge information about smuggling links with Serb-controlled territory.
"Plavsic has a point. She has put her finger on where it hurts," Carlos Westendorp, the international High Representative to Bosnia, told Reuters.
The same Western countries which condemned Plavsic's party during the war have decided to support her as she wages political battle with her former mentor Karadzic.
Balkan analysts say Plavsic is a nationalist with a reputation as a "true believer", who never joined the ruling Communist party of former Yugoslavia and was never implicated in corruption scandals.
"Critically, she cares about her people, perhaps not about others, but about her own," said Chris Bennett, author of "Yugoslavia's Bloody Collapse".
Plavsic has spoken admiringly of Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, who she sees as the kind of nationalist leader the Serbs lacked during during the Yugoslav conflict.
She refused to shake the hand of the patron of the Bosnian Serbs, Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic, when he tried to force them to accept a peace plan in 1993.
Milosevic has said nothing publicly about the power struggle but maintains close contacts with Karadzic's hardliners.

After Plavsic dissolved the Bosnian Serb parliament, Karadzic loyalists expected Milosevic to deliver the votes of Socialists at an assembly session called last week in defiance of the presidential order.

But the Socialist deputies never arrived and it remained unclear whether Milosevic would bail out the Pale leadership. Diplomats said it was the kind of political chaos that Milosevic has always thrived on.
"He relishes crises which he himself helped to create and which he plays an instrumental role in resolving," one said.
